title: Aaron Judge is back with Yankees. Here are 3 key questions for the team and its star
content:
On paper, the New York Yankees’ struggling lineup received the ultimate boost when the club activated Aaron Judge from the injured list Monday night.

In reality, there are questions Judge and the Yankees will need to answer, starting Tuesday night when he rejoins the team versus the Colorado Rockies at Yankee Stadium.

Here are three things we’re wondering:

The Yankees likely won’t use Judge at full speed right away. It has been 100 days since No. 99 has been in a major-league lineup, as he recovered from fracturing his first right rib while diving to make a catch. He attended the U.S. Open on Monday night, meaning he’s watched more live tennis matches (at least one) than he’s played rehab games (exactly zero). It was Judge’s choice to skip rehab games. On Aug. 27, he told reporters, “Why waste at-bats?”

“Why waste anything down in a minor-league game? I’ve been doing this for a while now, and I’ve got a sense of what I need to do on the field and how to manage it.”

Will Judge spend Tuesday as a designated hitter? Could the Yankees give him essentially a spring training plan on fast-forward, playing him in right field five innings for a couple of games, then seven innings for another few and then progress to full games? Everything seems to be on the table.

Saturday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Judge was “in a good spot.”

“He’s physically to the finish line,” the manager said, “where he needs to be. But it’s about just doing it a lot, because that’s ultimately what you’re trying to replicate is being out there for nine innings where you’re playing for three hours and sit down, get up — those kind of things. Just replicating that. So we’re getting to that point with the volume.”

Physically, Judge and the Yankees feel he’s prepared to face big-league pitching and play right field at Yankee Stadium.

But how quickly will Judge shake off his rust?

The 34-year-old has taken steps to get back to game speed, even facing live pitching at Yankee Stadium on Monday afternoon. Judge faced a righty and a lefty, according to video posted by MLB Network. He also stood at the plate with Max Fried on the mound Wednesday at Angel Stadium. Before the Yankees’ recent trip, he hit off the Trajekt high-velocity pitching machine, which uses a video board to simulate deliveries from major-league pitchers.

Judge also wasn’t able to perform over-the-head movements for a while as his rib recovered, which kept him out of the weight room. It’s unclear whether he’ll return with his usual power and tremendous bat speed.

“Even if it’s a tick off,” Judge said Aug. 27 regarding his bat speed, “I think it’s still better than nothing.”

A point in Judge’s favor? He didn’t play in any rehab games when he missed nearly two months with a toe injury in 2023, and he posted a .965 OPS over his final 57 games.

But at this point in the season, the talk around Judge is usually whether he’ll win another American League MVP, not whether he’ll have enough time to round into playoff shape.

The Yankees have 19 regular-season games remaining. They are four games back of the first-place Tampa Bay Rays and two games ahead of the third-place Boston Red Sox. The Yankees have a nine-game advantage in the wild-card standings, so they are a virtual lock to make the postseason.

Since June 2 — Judge’s first game out of the lineup — the Yankees have combined for a 90 wRC+, the second-worst mark in MLB, behind only the Los Angeles Angels (86). Over that span, they also ranked 26th in runs.

Before that, New York’s 116 wRC+ was second-best in the majors, and it had scored the fourth-most runs.

The Yankees can’t just hope Judge carries them. He’ll likely return to his customary No. 2 slot in the batting order. That could mean sandwiching lefties Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger around him, with Trent Grisham (right hamstring strain) on the injured list.

Rice has been on a tear lately, hitting .358 with a .943 OPS over his last 13 games. Bellinger has hit .293 with a .662 OPS in 14 games since coming off the IL after missing nearly a month with a left hamstring strain. Both should benefit from Judge’s presence.

The Yankees will also need Spencer Jones (.828 OPS over 39 games since being promoted July 26) to continue to hit and play a capable center field in Grisham’s absence.

“To have that right-handed hitter (Judge) on the days we’re facing a righty where we’ve got all our lefties in — to have a right-handed hitter in that two-three hole — I think it goes a long way,” Boone said, “not only having his production back in there, but hopefully putting other guys in a better spot.”
